extraction.name: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
extraction.description: MMMU is a benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: Our benchmark collection takes three stages. Firstly, we go through the common university majors to decide what subjects should be included in our benchmark. The selection is based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted in the subjects to provide valuable information. Through this principle, we rule out a few subjects like law and linguistics because it is difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems in these subjects. Consequently, we select 30 subjects from six different disciplines. In the second stage, we recruit over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to assist in question collection. They collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, as well as online resources. Annotators collected multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two steps of data cleaning were performed. In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity are employed to identify potential duplicate problems. These suspected duplicates were then reviewed by the authors to identify and eliminate any duplications. The second stage involves distributing the problems among different co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format. In the third and final stage, the authors categorize the problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects manually collected questions, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. Given arising data contamination concerns, annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers. Annotations must be accurate, consistent, and adhere to a high standard of academic rigor. All questions must contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, and not be ambiguous.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A user-friendly web interface was developed for data annotation and verification. Data is stored in JSON format.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A secondary review team rigorously vets annotations for quality and guideline adherence. Regular audits of random samples from the dataset are conducted to ensure sustained quality and consistency. Ambiguities or unclear data instances are flagged for a detailed review process and collaboratively examined in team meetings to establish a standardized approach for annotation.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in the 30 covered majors/subjects, drawn from various disciplines. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent a wide range of experts in the 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is divided into a few-shot development set (150 questions, 5 per subject), a validation set (~900 questions for hyperparameter selection), and a test set (10,500 questions). A live-updating leaderboard is available at https://mmmu-benchmark.github.io/#leaderboard. Version change logs are maintained (v1 Nov 2023 through v4 June 2024).
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotators were instructed to avoid collecting questions that contain any private information, in compliance with privacy laws and ethical standards in data handling.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark aims to monitor progress toward Expert AGI, which denotes an AI system that reaches 'at least 90th percentile of skilled adults' in a broad range of tasks. This could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption in many industries, making it of both intellectual and societal importance to closely monitor this progress.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The dataset excludes subjects like law and linguistics where finding enough relevant multimodal problems was difficult.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. However, strong performance on this benchmark should be a necessary criterion for an Expert AGI system.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It is used for benchmarking Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in a zero-shot setting. The dataset is divided into a few-shot development set (useful for in-context learning examples), a validation set (useful for hyperparameter selection), and a test set (used for final evaluation). Use cases include testing perception, knowledge recall, and reasoning capabilities of multimodal foundation models.
